subject: physics
title: Specific heat capacity and latent heat
key_idea: The energy to change a temperature depends on the mass, the specific heat capacity and the temperature change. The energy to change state depends on the mass and the specific latent heat. In a change of state the potential energy of the particles changes, not their kinetic energy.

sections.heading: Raising the temperature of a substance

blocks.text: Heating a substance raises its internal energy and, usually, its temperature. This section covers how much energy a given temperature rise needs.

items: Internal energy is the sum of the randomly distributed kinetic and potential energies of the particles in a body.
It increases when energy is transferred to the body by **heating**, or when **work** is done on it.
It decreases when energy is transferred out by heating, or when the body does work.

items: During a change of state the **potential energy** of the particles changes, because their separation changes.
The **kinetic energy** of the particles does not change, so the temperature stays constant.
Latent heat of vaporisation is much larger than that of fusion, because the particles move from close together to far apart.

items: Latent heat changes the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy.
Fusion is solid to liquid; vaporisation is liquid to gas.
Vaporisation needs far more energy per kilogram than fusion.

checks.q: Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
A solid melts at a steady rate while a heater supplies energy at a constant rate. Explain why its temperature stays constant.
checks.a: The energy supplied increases the potential energy of the particles as they move apart. Their kinetic energy does not change, so the temperature stays constant.

blocks.text: Internal energy and the first law

items: The internal energy of a system is increased when energy is transferred to it by heating or when work is done on it, and decreased in the opposite cases.
This is a qualitative form of the first law of thermodynamics.
During a change of state the potential energies of the particles change but their kinetic energies do not.
The two equations are also written Q = mcΔθ and Q = ml, where Q is the energy transferred and l is the specific latent heat.

Estimating c by the method of mixtures

items: Heat a metal sample of known mass to a known temperature, for example in boiling water.
Transfer it quickly into a known mass of cool water in an insulated container and stir.
Record the final steady temperature.
Energy lost by the metal equals energy gained by the water, assuming no losses, so c can be found.

blocks.text: Electrical method for a metal block

items: Place an electric heater and a thermometer in holes in an insulated metal block of known mass. A drop of oil in the thermometer hole improves thermal contact.
Record the potential difference V, current I, and the time t, or read the energy from a joulemeter.
Record the temperature rise Δθ and find c using the equation below.

blocks.label: Specific heat capacity, electrical method
where: m is the mass of the block (kg)

items: For a liquid, use a heater in a known mass of the liquid in an insulated container, and stir the liquid.
Lag the apparatus to reduce energy losses; losses make the calculated c too large.
A graph of temperature against time has a gradient of P / (mc) when the power P is steady.
Fusion: a heater sits in ice in a funnel and the melted water is collected and weighed. A control run with the heater off finds the melting caused by the room.
Vaporisation: a heater boils a liquid on a balance, and the loss in mass is measured over a known time.
To remove the effect of energy losses, repeat at two different powers P₁ and P₂ for the same time t.
Then L = (P₁ − P₂)t / (m₁ − m₂), where m₁ and m₂ are the masses that changed state.
